lessons.title: Solving quadratic equations exactly
lessons.summary: Choose factorisation, the quadratic formula or completing the square. Give every admissible root.
lessons.objective: Choose factorisation, the quadratic formula or completing the square. Give every admissible root.
lessons.before: Move all terms to one side. Look for a common factor or simple factors before using the formula.
lessons.ideas:
If a product is zero, at least one factor equals zero.

The formula is \(x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\) for a non-zero leading coefficient.

Factor an expression first and preserve all admissible inputs.
lessons.method:
Can I spot two linear factors?

Move all terms to one side. Look for a common factor or simple factors before using the formula.

What if the roots contain a square root?

Complete the square or use the quadratic formula. Preserve the exact radical.

Do I lose anything by dividing by x?

A common factor of x can equal zero. Set both factors equal to zero separately.
mistakes: Both factors can give roots. Keep a possible zero root.
Keep both signs and group the whole numerator over the denominator.
Dividing by x before considering x = 0 can discard a solution.

examples.title: Use a suitable method to solve a quadratic
examples.question:
The quadratic expression is \(F(x)=3 x^{2} - 3\).

Find all the real roots exactly.
examples.solution:
Rewrite as \(\left(x + 1\right) \left(3 x - 3\right)=0\) and apply the zero-product rule.

Solve both linear factors to obtain the complete root set.

Final answer: \(\{-1, 1\}\).

examples.title: Use a suitable method to solve a quadratic
examples.question:
The quadratic expression is \(F(x)=3 x^{2} - 12 x + 3\).

Find all the real roots exactly.
examples.solution:
Divide by the leading coefficient and complete the square.

The equation becomes \((x-2)^2=3\). Taking square roots gives both signs.

Final answer: \(\{2 - \sqrt{3}, \sqrt{3} + 2\}\).

examples.title: Use a suitable method to solve a quadratic
examples.question:
The quadratic expression is \(F(x)=3 x^{2} - 9 x\).

Find all the real roots exactly.
examples.solution:
Take out the common factor x and use the zero-product rule.

The factors are \(3 x \left(x - 3\right)\). The root at zero must be retained.

Final answer: \(\{0, 3\}\).

lessons.title: Completing the square and turning points
lessons.summary: Read a vertex, sketch the graph and give its range from completed-square form.
lessons.objective: Read a vertex, sketch the graph and give its range from completed-square form.
lessons.before: Take the leading coefficient out of the variable terms. Halve the new coefficient of x and square it.
lessons.ideas:
Restore the constant so the new expression expands to the starting one.

For \(a(x-h)^2+k\), the turning point is \((h,k)\).

An upward curve has a minimum. A downward curve has a maximum.
lessons.method:
How do I complete the square with a leading coefficient?

Take the leading coefficient out of the variable terms. Halve the new coefficient of x and square it.

How do the brackets identify the turning point?

Find the input where the square is zero. Take the output at that input as the second coordinate.

Does the vertex give a minimum or maximum?

The square is non-negative. Multiplying by a negative coefficient reflects the opening direction.
mistakes: Keep the outer coefficient when correcting the constant.
The horizontal coordinate is opposite to the sign shown in the bracket.
Give a range of outputs, with the turning-point value included.

examples.title: Complete the square and interpret the turning point
examples.question:
Let \(f(x)=2 x^{2} - 8 x + 4\).

Write an equivalent expression in completed-square form.
examples.solution:
Factor the leading coefficient from the quadratic and linear terms. Complete the square inside the bracket.

The horizontal offset is \(2\), yielding \(2 \left(x - 2\right)^{2} - 4\).

Final answer: \(2 \left(x - 2\right)^{2} - 4\).

examples.title: Complete the square and interpret the turning point
examples.question:
Let \(f(x)=2 x^{2} - 8 x + 8\).

Give the coordinates of the turning point.
examples.solution:
The square is zero at the horizontal coordinate of the turning point.

At \(x=2\), the minimum output is \(0\).

Final answer: \((2,0)\).

examples.title: Complete the square and interpret the turning point
examples.question:
Let \(f(x)=- 2 x^{2} + 12 x - 14\).

State the range for the domain of all real numbers.
examples.solution:
The sign of the leading coefficient determines which side of the vertex is reached.

The vertex gives the maximum value \(4\) and is attained.

Final answer: \(y\le 4\).

lessons.title: Quadratic range on a restricted domain
lessons.summary: Compare endpoints with any included turning point before writing a range.
lessons.objective: Compare endpoints with any included turning point before writing a range.
lessons.before: List the two included endpoints. Add the vertex if its input lies in the interval.
lessons.ideas:
The graph's extremes on a closed interval occur at the candidates listed.

A continuous curve on this closed interval takes every value between the two attained extremes.

Use the direction of opening as a check on your calculation.
lessons.method:
Which inputs can give the extremes?

List the two included endpoints. Add the vertex if its input lies in the interval.

How can I write the full range?

Calculate the smallest and largest outputs at the candidates.

How does a negative coefficient change the comparison?

The highest point may be inside the interval when the opening is downward. Compare both endpoints to find the lowest.
mistakes: A turning point may lie outside the domain.
The upper output need not come from the input endpoint furthest to the right.
Replacing x bounds by y bounds without evaluating them confuses domain with range.

examples.title: Compare the vertex and endpoints on a closed interval
examples.question:
The function \(f(x)=2 \left(x - 2\right)^{2} - 4\) has domain \(0\le x\le 7\) .

Find the value of \(x\) where the maximum occurs.
examples.solution:
Evaluate the two endpoints and the turning point, then compare outputs.

The three candidate values are \(4\), \(46\) and \(-4\). The right endpoint is farther from the vertex.

Final answer: \(7\).

examples.title: Compare the vertex and endpoints on a closed interval
examples.question:
The function \(f(x)=2 \left(x - 3\right)^{2}\) has domain \(0\le x\le 12\) .

State the full range.
examples.solution:
Use the smallest and the largest attained outputs.

The graph is continuous and takes every value from \(0\) to \(162\).

Final answer: \(0\le y\le 162\).

examples.solution:

The graph is continuous and takes every value from \(-94\) to \(4\).

Final answer: \(-94\le y\le 4\).

lessons.title: Discriminants and parameters
lessons.summary: Find when a parameter changes the number of real roots.
lessons.objective: Find when a parameter changes the number of real roots.
lessons.before: Read the three coefficients after putting zero on one side. Calculate the discriminant in terms of the parameter.
lessons.ideas:
Zero discriminant gives one repeated real root.

Use a strict inequality for two distinct roots.

No real roots means the discriminant is strictly negative.
lessons.method:
When are the roots equal?

Read the three coefficients after putting zero on one side. Calculate the discriminant in terms of the parameter.

When are there two distinct roots?

Solve the inequality that makes the expression below the square root positive.

When does a real root fail to exist?

A negative discriminant cannot have a real square root. Solve the inequality with the correct sign.
mistakes: Use the coefficient of x including its sign, and square that entire coefficient.
The repeated-root parameter belongs to a different case.
Reverse the inequality if dividing by a negative expression known to be constant.

examples.title: Use the discriminant to distinguish root cases
examples.question:
Consider \(2x^2-8x+k-2=0\), where \(k\) is a real constant.

Find \(k\) if the roots are equal.
examples.solution:
Equal roots occur when the discriminant is zero.

The discriminant is \(8(10-k)\) .

Final answer: \(10\).

examples.title: Use the discriminant to distinguish root cases
examples.question:
Consider \(1x^2-6x+k+2=0\), where \(k\) is a real constant.

Find the values of \(k\) for which there are two distinct real roots.
examples.solution:
Use a strictly positive discriminant.

The discriminant is \(4(7-k)\) .

Final answer: \(k<7\).

examples.title: Use the discriminant to distinguish root cases
examples.question:
Consider \(-5x^2+30x+k-1=0\), where \(k\) is a real constant.

Find the values of \(k\) for which there are no real roots.
examples.solution:
Use a negative discriminant.

The discriminant is \(20(k-(-44))\) .

Final answer: \(k<-44\).

lessons.title: Quadratic inequalities and sign diagrams
lessons.summary: Find all intervals, including the correct endpoint choices and repeated-root cases.
lessons.objective: Find all intervals, including the correct endpoint choices and repeated-root cases.
lessons.before: Find the roots and mark them on the axis. Check whether each region lies above or below.
lessons.ideas:
A quadratic with positive leading coefficient is negative between its distinct roots and positive outside.

A non-strict sign includes the two boundary points. A strict sign excludes them.

A non-negative perfect square has one zero and is positive elsewhere.
lessons.method:
Which parts of the graph satisfy an inequality?

Find the roots and mark them on the axis. Check whether each region lies above or below.

When do I include a root?

Evaluate the original statement at equality. Include a root when equality satisfies the inequality.

What if the graph only touches the axis?

A repeated root touches the axis and does not change the sign of the quadratic.
mistakes: Check the leading sign before choosing the central interval.
For separate intervals, use or to join them.
Do not introduce a sign change at a double root.

examples.title: Use two zeros to solve a quadratic inequality
examples.question:
The quadratic expression is \(g(x)=2 x^{2} - 8\).

Solve \(g(x)<0\).
examples.solution:
Mark the roots and check the sign in each region.

The solution lies between the roots. Exclude equality at either root.

Final answer: \(-2

examples.title: Use two zeros to solve a quadratic inequality
examples.question:
The quadratic expression is \(g(x)=2 x^{2} + 6 x - 36\).

Solve \(g(x)\ge0\).
examples.solution:
Mark the roots and check the sign in each region.

The solution lies outside the roots. Include equality at either root.

Final answer: \(x\le -6\) or \(x\ge 3\).

examples.title: Handle a repeated root in an inequality
examples.question:
Let \(q(x)=3 x^{2} - 24 x + 48\).

Find the solution set of \(q(x)>0\).
examples.solution:
Use the fact that a perfect square is non-negative.

A repeated root touches the horizontal axis. The sign elsewhere does not change.

Final answer: \(x\ne 4\).

lessons.title: Simultaneous linear and quadratic equations
lessons.summary: Substitute one equation into the other and recover all matching coordinates.
lessons.objective: Substitute one equation into the other and recover all matching coordinates.
lessons.before: Both equations specify the same output at an intersection. Substitute using the simpler equation.
lessons.ideas:
An equal-output equation reduces the problem to one variable.

Report both ordered pairs when there are two intersections.

Take the absolute value of the difference to express a distance.
lessons.method:
How can I remove the y-variable?

Both equations specify the same output at an intersection. Substitute using the simpler equation.

How do I keep the coordinates paired correctly?

Work with one root at a time. Use the line to find the matching y-coordinate and check the curve.

Can I measure how far apart the graphs are?

Use one x-coordinate for both outputs. A vertical separation is the positive difference between outputs.
mistakes: Write which two expressions are equal before expanding.
Two lists of coordinates are ambiguous unless the matching pairs are clear.
A horizontal separation measures a different quantity.

examples.title: Find both intersections and verify the ordered pairs
examples.question:
Solve the simultaneous equations \(y=2 x + 1\) and \(y=2 x^{2} + 4 x - 11\).

Find the set of possible x-coordinates.
examples.solution:
Both equations describe the same y-value at an intersection. Set their right sides equal.

The difference factorises as \(\left(x - 2\right) \left(2 x + 6\right)\).

Final answer: \(\{-3, 2\}\).

examples.title: Find both intersections and verify the ordered pairs
examples.question:
Solve the simultaneous equations \(y=- x - 3\) and \(y=3 x^{2} - x - 30\).

Give all solutions as ordered pairs.
examples.solution:
Substitute each root in the linear equation.

The two y-values are \(0\) and \(-6\). Check either original equation.

Final answer: \((-3,0),\quad (3,-6)\).

examples.title: Find both intersections and verify the ordered pairs
examples.question:
Solve the simultaneous equations \(y=5 x\) and \(y=x^{2} + 5 x - 9\).

Find the vertical separation at the average of the two x-coordinates.
examples.solution:
Subtract the two outputs at the same input. Take the absolute value for the separation.

Evaluate the difference at \(0\).

Final answer: \(9\).

lessons.title: Simultaneous nonlinear systems
lessons.summary: Choose a substitution or divide safely when two nonlinear equations share a factor.
lessons.objective: Choose a substitution or divide safely when two nonlinear equations share a factor.
lessons.before: Use the sum to express one variable in terms of the other. Substitute in the product equation.
lessons.ideas:
The two roots may give two ordered pairs with the coordinates exchanged.

A known non-zero product can be used as a divisor.

After solving the substituted equation, recover both original variables subject to all denominator restrictions.
lessons.method:
How can a sum and product give two variables?

Use the sum to express one variable in terms of the other. Substitute in the product equation.

When is it safe to divide two equations?

Check whether the common expression is non-zero from the stated data.

Which substitution works for ratios?

Spot ratios that are reciprocals. Take one ratio as a new unknown and express all other ratios using it.
mistakes: Record each valid pair even when both pairs contain the same numbers.
Before dividing by an expression, explain how zero is ruled out.
A root of the substituted equation is not yet the requested ordered pair.

examples.title: Choose a substitution or division for a nonlinear system
examples.question:
Solve the system \(x+y=7\), \(xy=12\) .

Give the complete set of ordered pairs.
examples.solution:
Use each result to find its corresponding y-value, then check both original equations.

The admissible pairs are \((3,4),\quad (4,3)\). Any forbidden zero in a denominator is excluded.

Final answer: \((3,4),\quad (4,3)\).

examples.title: Choose a substitution or division for a nonlinear system
examples.question:

Find every possible x-coordinate.
examples.solution:
Reduce the system to one unknown before solving.

Since \(xy=8\ne0\), division gives \(y=32/8=4\) . Then use the first equation.

Final answer: \(\{2\}\).

A strictly positive discriminant gives two distinct intersection points.
lessons.method:
How do I recognise tangency algebraically?

Set the line and curve outputs equal. Use the fact that the resulting quadratic has a repeated root.

What are the tangent point's coordinates?

Use the repeated intersection input to find its output from either equation.

How does shifting the line change the number of intersections?

Compare the line intercept with its value at tangency. A small sketch can confirm which direction produces two crossings.
mistakes: Use the discriminant of the intersection equation.
Give both x and y when the question asks for a point.
The boundary value is excluded when there must be two crossings.

examples.title: Find a tangent in a family of parallel lines
examples.question:
The curve is \(y=2 \left(x - 2\right)^{2} - 3\). The line has equation \(y=8 x+k\) for constant \(k\).

Find \(k\) when the line is tangent.
examples.solution:
Equate the curve to the line. At tangency the resulting quadratic has a repeated root.

The square term is centred at \(4\). Requiring its remaining constant to vanish gives \(-27\).

Final answer: \(-27\).

examples.title: Find a tangent in a family of parallel lines
examples.question:

examples.solution:
The repeated root gives the x-coordinate. Substitute it into either equation.

At \(4\), the curve has output \(-1\).

Final answer: \((4,-1)\).

examples.title: Find a tangent in a family of parallel lines
examples.question:
The curve is \(y=2 \left(x - 4\right)^{2} - 4\). The line has equation \(y=20 x+k\) for constant \(k\).

Find the intercepts k for which there are two distinct intersections.
examples.solution:
The horizontal shift in the level must give a strictly positive squared offset.

The equation rearranges to \(2 \left(x - 9\right)^{2}=k-(-134)\) . Divide by the signed leading coefficient.

Final answer: \(k>-134\).

Solve the simultaneous equations \(y=- 3 x - 2\) and \(y=x^{2} - 21 x - 90\).

  1. Find the set of possible x-coordinates.

    [2]

  2. Give all solutions as ordered pairs.

    [2]

  3. Find the vertical separation at the average of the two x-coordinates.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Both equations describe the same y-value at an intersection. Set their right sides equal.

The difference factorises as \(\left(x - 22\right) \left(x + 4\right)\).

Final answer: \(\{-4, 22\}\).

(b)

Substitute each root in the linear equation.

The two y-values are \(10\) and \(-68\). Check either original equation.

Final answer: \((-4,10),\quad (22,-68)\).

(c)

Subtract the two outputs at the same input. Take the absolute value for the separation.

Evaluate the difference at \(9\).

Final answer: \(169\).
